opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when I started, around 2009 or 2010, the landscape was pretty fragmented and honestly pretty small. Deep learning wasn't mainstream yet, so there wasn't really a "framework landscape" in the sense people think of it today. There were a handful of research labs, and each one had its own tooling.

At NYU, in Yann LeCun's lab, there was a lineage of tools. There was Lush, a Lisp-based environment that Yann and Léon Bottou had built, and there was EBLearn, a C++ library. Then there was Torch, which had come out of Ronan Collobert's work and was maintained by Ronan, Koray Kavukcuoglu, and Clément Farabet, and it used Lua. Over in Montreal, Yoshua Bengio's group had Theano, which was quite forward-looking. It had symbolic graphs and automatic differentiation, and it compiled things down. Then a bit later you had things like cuda-convnet from Alex Krizhevsky, and then Caffe out of Berkeley, which really took off for computer vision.

So it was very much a world where the tool you used was tied to the lab you came from. There wasn't one dominant thing. People weren't thinking much about usability or about a broad user base, because the user base was maybe a few hundred people. You built what you needed to get your experiments done, and if a few other people found it useful, great.

What was interesting was that you could already see a split in philosophy. Some tools leaned toward the compiler approach: define a graph, optimize it, run it. Others, like Torch, were more imperative. You just wrote code, it ran, and you could poke at it. That tension carried forward for years and shaped a lot of what came after.

I was mostly a user at first. I was just trying to train convnets and get things working on GPUs, and a lot of my time went into fighting the tools rather than doing the research. That frustration ended up being pretty formative for me.

r001.rationale: It names frameworks using Lisp, C++, and Lua, clearly showing that the early ecosystem spanned multiple programming languages.

r002.rationale: It says tools came from research labs and names maintainers, but does not state that frameworks were typically developed by only a couple of graduate students.

r003.rationale: It describes a philosophical split between compiler-based and imperative tools, but does not place this at Soumith’s joining FAIR or say frameworks were competing by trying to differentiate themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
When I started, around 2010 or 2011, the landscape was pretty fragmented and honestly pretty hostile to someone who just wanted to try ideas quickly. The dominant option in a lot of academic labs was Theano, out of Montreal, and Theano was really ahead of its time in some ways, because it had automatic differentiation and symbolic graphs, but it also had this painful compile step. You'd write your model, hit run, and then wait a minute or more for it to compile before you could even find out that you had a shape mismatch. So the iteration loop was slow, and that shaped how people worked.

Then there was Torch, the Lua-based framework that came out of the Yann LeCun and Ronan Collobert lineage, which I ended up spending a lot of my time on at NYU and later at Facebook. Torch had the opposite philosophy. It was very imperative, very hands-on. You wrote the forward pass, and you also often wrote the backward pass yourself, module by module. That was more work, but it meant the thing you wrote was the thing that ran. There was no magic in between you and the computation, which researchers loved, because when you're doing weird new architectures, magic tends to get in your way.

And then around the edges you had Caffe out of Berkeley, which was fantastic if you wanted to train a convnet from a config file and get a result quickly, but much harder if you wanted to do anything that wasn't a feedforward conv net. You had a lot of people writing custom CUDA code by hand. You had Matlab still being used in a surprising number of labs. People were rolling their own things constantly.

The thing I'd say characterizes that whole era is that the frameworks were built by researchers for themselves, and each one encoded a very particular view of what research looked like. Theano assumed you wanted to describe a graph and optimize it. Caffe assumed you wanted to stack layers. Torch assumed you wanted total control and were willing to pay for it in boilerplate. None of them really assumed that you'd want to debug with a print statement, or step through your model in a debugger, or that non-experts would ever use them. And when TensorFlow arrived in late 2015, it came from a very industrial place, with the graph abstraction taken even further, which was great for deployment at Google scale but made the research experience feel even more remote. A lot of what eventually became PyTorch was really a reaction to all of that, trying to keep the directness of Torch while borrowing the things that made Python and NumPy so pleasant to work in.

r001.rationale: The response names frameworks and tools associated with Lua, Matlab, Python/NumPy, and CUDA, characterizing an ecosystem that spanned multiple programming languages.

r002.rationale: It says frameworks were built by researchers for themselves, but does not state they were typically developed by only a couple of graduate students.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts frameworks’ different philosophies and capabilities, but does not characterize them as competing through attempts to differentiate themselves.

astra-6.text:
When I started doing research, the landscape was pretty fragmented. You’d often get code that was written specifically for a paper, and getting it running—or adapting it to your own idea—could take a lot of work. People used MATLAB, wrote C or C++, and built their own infrastructure. There wasn’t really a common foundation everyone agreed on.

Then you had tools like Theano and Torch that made it easier to express models and reuse components. But choosing a framework still meant choosing a particular way of working, and often a particular community. It felt much more like a collection of research tools than the mature software ecosystem we think of today.

r001.rationale: It names MATLAB, C, and C++ as languages people used, clearly showing the ecosystem spanned multiple programming languages.

r002.rationale: It says researchers built their own infrastructure but does not state that frameworks were typically developed by only a couple of graduate students.

r003.rationale: It says frameworks represented different ways of working and communities, but does not describe frameworks competing by trying to differentiate themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
When I started doing research, the framework landscape was pretty fragmented. You’d often download code that came with a paper and spend a lot of time getting it to run, then modify it for your own experiments. There wasn’t this expectation that you could pick one framework and have a whole ecosystem around it.

Theano and Torch were emerging as useful options, but they had different philosophies. Theano was about describing a computation symbolically and compiling it, while Torch felt more like a numerical programming library where you wrote the program directly. And plenty of people were still writing their own C++ or CUDA, or working in MATLAB.

So choosing your tools was a pretty substantial part of doing research. You were thinking about what you could actually implement and debug, alongside the research question itself.

r001.rationale: It names Theano, Torch, C++, CUDA, and MATLAB, conveying an ecosystem spread across multiple programming languages and tools.

r002.rationale: It does not say that frameworks were typically developed by a couple of graduate students.

r003.rationale: It notes that Theano and Torch had different philosophies, but does not describe frameworks around Soumith’s arrival at FAIR competing to differentiate themselves.
